region: Western North America; widely planted in Europe and New Zealand
description: Douglas fir is a strong, stiff softwood used for structural beams, framing, flooring, joinery and plywood. Its orange-brown heartwood and bold growth rings make it popular for timber framing and furniture too.

hazards.summary: The UK HSE lists Douglas fir as a cause of dermatitis. It does not say whether this is irritation or allergy, and we found no primary case reports.
The UK HSE notes that Douglas fir splinters can become infected (go septic). Remove splinters promptly and clean the wound.
The UK HSE lists runny or blocked nose and effects on the airways from Douglas fir dust. No primary study confirming an allergy was found.
All wood dust is classified as carcinogenic to humans, mainly linked to cancers of the nose and sinuses. This applies to this wood like every other species.

Very pronounced flat-sawn growth rings with a sharp contrast between pale earlywood and dark reddish latewood, forming bold cathedral arches, medium texture, moderate resinous sheen and no visible pores. No text, no logos, no hands, no tools, no finish or varnish, natural unfinished wood. Wide 1200x630 composition (1.91:1) with the board centered and margin on both sides for cropping.

notes_internal: Botanical name verified on WFO as accepted Pseudotsuga menziesii (Mirb.) Franco. All hazards rest on HSE-WIS30 alone; PubMed searches (Douglas fir / Pseudotsuga with dermatitis, allergy, asthma) returned only tussock moth reports, not wood. Schlunssen-2018 mentions Douglas fir only as one extract in a Carosso et al. study (not tabulated). source_part for splinters set to heartwood as a judgment; HSE does not specify.
